data.name: Light_Brightness_P1
data.value: A lamp turns electricity into light. Double its power and twice as much light lands on the floor, yet the floor does not look twice as bright. Try it: the first few watts make a big difference, the last few hardly any.

data.name: Light_Brightness_P2
data.value: Our eyes, and the screens made for them, squeeze large amounts of light together. Keep turning it up and the floor under the lamp simply turns white: a screen cannot show anything brighter than its white.

data.name: Light_Brightness_Deeper
data.value: The picture adds light up as it really is, then bends it with the screen's curve (roughly the 1/2.2 power) just before it is shown. The chart shows that curve and where the floor under the lamp is on it.

data.name: Light_Brightness_Picture
data.value: A small lamp over a floor, with a chart of how bright the light looks

data.name: Light_Tilt_P1
data.value: Shine a torch straight down on a board, then tip the board. The beam has not changed, but it now lands on a longer patch, so every bit of the patch gets a smaller share of the light.

data.name: Light_Tilt_P2
data.value: At 60° the patch is twice as long, so it is half as bright. Tip it right over and the light just slides past. This is why sunlight warms the ground more at noon than in the evening, when it comes in low.

data.name: Light_Tilt_Deeper
data.value: Brightness = straight-on brightness × cos(angle). The patch is 1 / cos(angle) times as long.

data.name: Light_Tilt_Picture
data.value: A torch shining down on a tilting board, seen from the side

data.name: Light_Distance_P1
data.value: A small lamp sends light out in every direction. Follow just the light that passes through one square a metre away. At 2 metres that same light covers 4 such squares, at 3 metres 9.

data.name: Light_Distance_P2
data.value: Spread over more squares, each square gets less: at twice the distance, a quarter of the light. Sound from a small speaker thins out the same way.

data.name: Light_Distance_Deeper
data.value: Brightness ∝ 1 / distance². This is the inverse-square law; it holds for a lamp that is small next to the distance.

data.name: Light_Distance_Picture
data.value: A lamp and the light through one square, spreading over more squares further away

data.name: Light_Distance_Readout
data.value: The light covers {0} squares · each gets {1}%

data.name: Light_Angle_P1
data.value: A car down the road looks smaller than the same car parked next to you. What your eye takes in is not how long the car is but the angle between its two ends.

data.name: Light_Angle_P2
data.value: Draw a circle round your eye: the arc between the two lines, divided by the circle's radius, is that angle in radians. Twice as far, half the angle. For a patch instead of a line the same idea is the solid angle: how much of your view it fills.

data.name: Light_Angle_Deeper
data.value: Angle in radians = arc ÷ radius. A full turn is 2π ≈ 6.28 radians; far away, the angle ≈ size ÷ distance.

data.name: Light_Angle_Picture
data.value: From above: an eye, a car down the road and the angle between its ends

data.name: Light_Shadow_P1
data.value: A lamp hangs over a box. Stand anywhere on the floor and ask: how much of the lamp can I see past the box? Where it is all hidden, the shadow is full; where only part of it is hidden, the shadow is part dark.

data.name: Light_Shadow_P2
data.value: A small lamp is hidden all at once, so its shadow has a sharp edge. A big lamp, or a cloudy sky, is hidden a little at a time, so the edge fades gently. Raise the lamp, grow it, move it aside, and watch the edge.

data.name: Light_Shadow_Deeper
data.value: The fully dark part is the umbra, the soft edge the penumbra. The picture works out, for every point of the floor, how much of the lamp it can see.

data.name: Light_Shadow_Picture
data.value: A square lamp over a floor with a box on it

data.name: Light_Sky_Title
data.value: What a spot on the floor sees

data.name: Light_Sky_P1
data.value: Put your eye on a spot of the floor and look up: you see a half-sphere of sky. The lamp is one patch of it. Now press that half-sphere flat onto the floor, like a dome squashed into a circle: the lamp's patch lands somewhere in the circle.

data.name: Light_Sky_P2
data.value: The share of the circle the lamp covers is the share of light the spot gets. A low lamp squashes thin near the rim — that is the slant of spread 2 — and a far lamp shrinks — that is the distance of spread 3. One picture holds both.

data.name: Light_Sky_Deeper
data.value: Light received ∝ the patch's size on the sky (its solid angle) × cos(how far from overhead). Pressing the dome flat does that multiplication for you.

data.name: Light_Sky_Share
data.value: The lamp covers {0}% of the circle

data.name: Light_Sky_Picture
data.value: A spot on the floor, the half-sphere of sky over it, and a lamp pressed onto both

data.name: Light_Sky_Readout
data.value: The lamp covers {0}% of the circle: that share of a whole sky's light

data.name: Light_Radiance_Title
data.value: Why a wall looks as bright from far away

data.name: Light_Radiance_P1
data.value: Walk away from a lit wall and it does not get dimmer. Odd, since each bit of it now sends you less light. But each speck of your eye now takes in more of the wall: twice as far, four times as much wall, each part a quarter as bright to you.

data.name: Light_Radiance_P2
data.value: Turn the panel away and the same thing happens: the eye takes in more of it, and a matte surface sends less light off at a slant, by just as much. What stays the same is how bright the surface looks — its radiance — which is what eyes and cameras measure.

data.name: Light_Radiance_Deeper
data.value: Area seen ∝ distance² / cos, light from each bit ∝ cos / distance²: the product is 1. A surface that holds this at every angle is called Lambertian.

data.name: Light_Radiance_Picture
data.value: From the side: an eye's narrow cone of view meeting a glowing panel

data.name: Light_Radiance_PerBit
data.value: Light from each bit that reaches the eye: {0}×

data.name: Light_Reflection_P1
data.value: Light that lands on a surface leaves it again, but where it goes depends on the surface. A mirror sends it all on in one direction, as a ball bounces off a wall. A matte surface, like paper, scatters it every way.

data.name: Light_Reflection_P2
data.value: Most things are in between: glossy paint, a polished table. Move the eye: on a mirror you see the lamp only from one place; on paper the spot looks about the same from everywhere; on gloss you see a bright highlight that follows you.

data.name: Light_Reflection_Deeper
data.value: The shape over the surface shows how much light leaves in each direction. For a matte surface it is a circle (cos of the angle from straight up); for a mirror, a single spike at the mirror angle.

data.name: Light_Reflection_Picture
data.value: From the side: light landing on a surface and the shape of the light leaving it

data.name: Light_Bounce_P1
data.value: A red wall is red because it gives back mostly red light and keeps the rest. White gives back all colours. With no bounces, only what the lamp reaches is lit, and the box's shadow side is pitch black.

data.name: Light_Bounce_P2
data.value: Add a bounce: everything lit now lights everything else. The floor near the wall turns faintly red, and shadows fill in. A second and third bounce add less each time. This is why rooms are never as dark in the shade as the lamp alone would make them.

data.name: Light_Bounce_Deeper
data.value: Each bounce passes light between every pair of points: how much one sends, times how squarely the two face each other, over the distance squared. Computer graphics calls this radiosity, or global illumination.

data.name: Light_Bounce_Picture
data.value: A lamp over a white floor and box beside a coloured wall

data.name: Gears_Ratio_P1
data.value: Press two wheels together and turn one: the other turns the opposite way. Where they touch, both rims move the same distance, so the small wheel has to spin round more times to keep up with the big one.

data.name: Gears_Ratio_P2
data.value: Smooth wheels slip once the load gets heavy. Teeth stop that: each tooth pushes into a gap on the other wheel, so the two can never slide past each other, and counting teeth tells you exactly how their speeds compare.

data.name: Gears_Ratio_Deeper
data.value: Turns of the driven gear = turns of the driving gear × driving teeth ÷ driven teeth. The dashed circles are the rolling circles (pitch circles): the two smooth wheels that the gears behave like.

data.name: Gears_Ratio_Readout
data.value: For each turn of the gold gear, the grey one turns {0} times.

data.name: Gears_Ratio_Picture
data.value: Two gears in mesh: the gold one drives the grey one

data.name: Gears_Torque_P1
data.value: Gears cannot make something out of nothing. When a small gear drives a big one, the big gear turns slower, and in return it turns harder. The teeth push on each other equally hard, but the big gear feels that push further from its centre, like a longer spanner.

data.name: Gears_Torque_P2
data.value: That is how a hand crank lifts a heavy load: a small gear turns a big drum gear, trading speed for force. Run it the other way round and you trade force for speed, which is what a bicycle does when its big front sprocket spins the small back one fast.

data.name: Gears_Torque_Deeper
data.value: Turning force (torque) = push × distance from the centre. With 3 times as many teeth, the drum turns 3 times slower and 3 times harder: speed × turning force stays the same, apart from what friction takes.

data.name: Gears_Torque_Readout
data.value: The drum turns at {0} times the crank's speed, with {1} times its turning force.

data.name: Gears_Torque_Picture
data.value: A hand crank on a small gear turns a big gear with a drum that lifts a weight

data.name: Gears_Involute_P1
data.value: Wind a string round a can, tie a pencil to its end and unwind it, keeping the string tight. The pencil draws a curve that spirals away from the can. Good gear teeth have exactly this curve on both sides. It is called an involute.

data.name: Gears_Involute_P2
data.value: Why that curve? The tight string always meets the curve at a right angle. So when two such teeth press on each other, the push always runs along one straight line, at one angle, however far the gears have turned. The gears turn smoothly, without tugging or rattling.

data.name: Gears_Involute_Deeper
data.value: The can is the gear's base circle. The string that has come off is as long as the arc of the can it came off, so the pencil moves away steadily as you unwind.

data.name: Gears_Involute_Picture
data.value: A string unwound from a can; its end draws the curve of a gear tooth

data.name: Gears_Involute_Ghost
data.value: Faint: a gear whose tooth has this curve as its side

data.name: Gears_Mesh_P1
data.value: Watch the gold dots: they mark where teeth are touching. Each one slides along the same slanted line, from where a pair of teeth first meet to where they let go. Before one pair lets go, the next pair has already met, so the push never stops.

data.name: Gears_Mesh_P2
data.value: The slant of that line is the pressure angle. A bigger angle makes teeth stubbier and stronger but pushes the gears apart harder; a smaller one is gentler but the teeth are thinner. Most gears today use 20°.

data.name: Gears_Mesh_Deeper
data.value: The line of action touches both base circles. It crosses the line between the centres at the pitch point, where the two rolling circles meet, and the push between the teeth always points along it.

data.name: Gears_Mesh_Readout
data.value: On average {0} pairs of teeth are touching.

data.name: Gears_Mesh_Picture
data.value: Two gears turning slowly, with the line of action and the points where teeth touch

data.name: Gears_Train_P1
data.value: One pair of gears can only slow things down so far before the big gear gets enormous. Instead, fix a small gear to the big one's axle and let it drive the next big gear. Each step multiplies the slowing.

data.name: Gears_Train_P2
data.value: Here every step turns the speed down 3 times. Two steps make 9, three make 27, four make 81. A clock uses steps like these to turn one fast shaft into a second hand, a minute hand and an hour hand.

data.name: Gears_Train_Deeper
data.value: Total ratio = ratio of step 1 × ratio of step 2 × … A small gear and a big gear on one axle (a compound gear) turn together, at the same speed.

data.name: Gears_Train_Readout
data.value: The last gear turns once for every {0} turns of the first.

data.name: Gears_Train_Picture
data.value: A gear train: small gears on the same axles as big ones, each driving the next

data.name: Gears_Planet_P1
data.value: A sun gear sits in the middle, planet gears roll round it, and a ring with teeth on the inside holds them all. A frame, the carrier (the triangle), holds the planets' axles. Hold one of the three parts still, turn another, and the third comes out at a new speed.

data.name: Gears_Planet_P2
data.value: Hold the ring and the carrier creeps round slowly: a big reduction in a small space. Hold the carrier instead and the ring turns backwards. Car gearboxes, electric screwdrivers and bicycle hub gears switch between these just by braking different parts.

data.name: Gears_Planet_Deeper
data.value: Sun teeth × sun turns + ring teeth × ring turns = (sun teeth + ring teeth) × carrier turns. The part held makes 0 turns, and the other two follow from that.

data.name: Gears_Planet_Readout
data.value: Turn the {0} once and the {1} turns {2} times.

data.name: Gears_Planet_ReadoutBack
data.value: Turn the {0} once and the {1} turns {2} times, backwards.

data.name: Gears_Planet_Picture
data.value: A planetary gear set: a sun, three planets on a carrier, and a ring

data.name: Watch_Spring_P1
data.value: A mechanical watch has no battery. Its energy is a long, thin strip of steel, the mainspring, coiled up inside a little drum called the barrel. Turning the crown winds the spring tight round the arbor in the middle.

data.name: Watch_Spring_P2
data.value: Left alone, the spring tries to uncoil and pushes the barrel round. The barrel has teeth on its rim, and they drive all the other wheels. A full spring keeps a watch like this one going for about 40 hours.

data.name: Watch_Spring_Deeper
data.value: The spring pulls hardest when it is full and less as it runs down. On its own that would make the watch run fast, then slow; the part on the next pages that lets the energy out a little at a time is what keeps the rate steady.

data.name: Watch_Spring_Readout
data.value: Enough for about {0} hours: the barrel can still turn {1} times.

data.name: Watch_Spring_Picture
data.value: The mainspring coiled in its barrel, seen from above, with gauges for its pull and the hours left

data.name: Watch_Hands_Title
data.value: From one spring to three hands

data.name: Watch_Hands_P1
data.value: Between the barrel and the hands is a row of wheels, the going train. Each big wheel drives a small pinion on the next axle, so each axle turns faster than the one before. The centre wheel turns once an hour and carries the minute hand; the fourth wheel turns once a minute and carries the seconds hand.

data.name: Watch_Hands_P2
data.value: The hour hand is not on this train at all. Under the dial, a few more small wheels slow the minute hand down twelve times, so the hour hand goes once round while the minute hand goes round twelve times.

data.name: Watch_Hands_Deeper
data.value: Barrel 80 teeth → centre pinion 10: the barrel turns once every 8 hours. Centre 64 → 8, third 60 → 8, fourth 80 → 8: 8 × 7.5 × 10 = 600 turns of the escape wheel an hour.

data.name: Watch_Hands_Picture
data.value: A watch dial and, below, the row of wheels from the barrel to the escape wheel

data.name: Watch_Escape_P1
data.value: Left to itself, the spring would whirl the wheels round and run down in seconds. The escapement stops that. A lever with two red stones holds the escape wheel still; each time the balance swings past the middle, it flicks the lever across, one stone lets go, the wheel jumps half a tooth, and the other stone catches it. That jump is the tick you hear.

data.name: Watch_Escape_P2
data.value: The wheel does not just get let go: as it slips past a stone, its tooth gives the lever a small push, and the lever passes it on to the balance. That push, once a beat, keeps the balance swinging for as long as the spring lasts.

data.name: Watch_Escape_Deeper
data.value: Two beats per tooth, 15 teeth per turn, 10 turns a minute: 300 beats a minute, 18,000 an hour. The balance is free for most of each swing and touches the lever only near the middle, which is why this kind is called a detached lever escapement.

data.name: Watch_Escape_Picture
data.value: The lever escapement in slow motion: balance, lever with two stones, escape wheel

data.name: Watch_Balance_P1
data.value: What sets the pace is the balance: a little wheel on a hair-thin spiral spring. Turn it and the spring pulls it back; it overshoots, the spring pulls the other way, and it swings to and fro like a swing in a playground, two and a half times a second.

data.name: Watch_Balance_P2
data.value: The trick is that a wide swing and a narrow swing take the same time: a wider swing just moves faster. So as the spring runs down and the pushes get weaker, the watch keeps its rate. A stiffer hairspring, though, speeds it up, and a few tenths of a percent is minutes a day.

data.name: Watch_Balance_Deeper
data.value: Swings a second = √(spring stiffness ÷ heaviness of the wheel) ÷ 2π. The swing's width is not in it. Watchmakers adjust the rate by changing how much of the hairspring is free to bend.

data.name: Watch_Balance_Readout
data.value: {0} swings a second ({1} beats an hour).

data.name: Watch_Balance_Gains
data.value: The watch would gain {0} minutes a day.

data.name: Watch_Balance_Loses
data.value: The watch would lose {0} minutes a day.

data.name: Watch_Balance_Picture
data.value: The balance wheel and its hairspring swinging, with a trace of its angle over time

data.name: Watch_Rotor_P1
data.value: An automatic watch winds itself. Behind the movement hangs a heavy half-moon, the rotor, free to swing on the centre. Every time the wrist moves, gravity keeps the rotor hanging down while the watch turns round it, and that swinging winds the mainspring.

data.name: Watch_Rotor_P2
data.value: The rotor swings both ways, but the spring only winds one way. A reverser, a pair of one-way clutches, turns both directions into winding. Once the spring is full, a slipping spring in the barrel lets it slide instead of breaking.

data.name: Watch_Rotor_Deeper
data.value: Without the reverser only half the swings count. Try it: with a lazy wrist, the watch then uses its spring faster than the rotor can fill it.

data.name: Watch_Rotor_Picture
data.value: The back of an automatic watch: a swinging rotor winds the mainspring

data.name: Watch_Movement_P1
data.value: Here is everything together, pulled apart so you can see each layer. At the bottom, the main plate holds every axle in tiny ruby bearings. Above it, the barrel with its spring, the going train, then the escapement and balance.

data.name: Watch_Movement_P2
data.value: On top sit the motion works, the small wheels that make the hour hand, and then the dial and hands. Hide the layers one by one and follow the energy from the spring at the bottom up to the hands at the top.

data.name: Watch_Movement_Deeper
data.value: Real movements spread these parts out side by side under bridges rather than stacking them, so the watch stays thin. Rubies are used for bearings because they are very hard and very smooth, so the steel pivots hardly wear.

data.name: Watch_Movement_Picture
data.value: The watch movement taken apart into layers, seen from the side and above

data.name: Narr_Light_Brightness_01
data.value: Here the lamp is turned down low, and only a dim pool of light reaches the floor.

data.name: Narr_Light_Brightness_02
data.value: Double the power. Twice as much light lands on the floor, and the pool brightens a lot.

data.name: Narr_Light_Brightness_03
data.value: Now it is eight times that. More light again, yet the floor hardly looks brighter than before.

data.name: Narr_Light_Brightness_04
data.value: So when twice as much light reaches the floor, does the floor look twice as bright?

data.name: Narr_Light_Brightness_05
data.value: Your turn: turn the lamp all the way up and watch what happens under it.

data.name: Narr_Light_Tilt_01
data.value: The beam comes straight down, so the lit patch on the board is just as wide as the beam.

data.name: Narr_Light_Tilt_02
data.value: Tip the board. The same beam now lands on a longer patch, so each part of it gets less.

data.name: Narr_Light_Tilt_03
data.value: Your turn: tip the board to sixty degrees and read how long the patch gets.

data.name: Narr_Light_Tilt_04
data.value: The patch is now twice as long. How bright is each bit of it?

data.name: Narr_Light_Distance_01
data.value: Follow the light that goes through one square, one metre from the lamp.

data.name: Narr_Light_Distance_02
data.value: At two metres that same light spreads over four squares, so each one gets a quarter.

data.name: Narr_Light_Distance_03
data.value: At three metres it covers nine squares.

data.name: Narr_Light_Distance_04
data.value: So at three metres, how much light does each square get, compared with one metre?

data.name: Narr_Light_Angle_01
data.value: The car is close, so in your view its two ends are far apart: a wide angle.

data.name: Narr_Light_Angle_02
data.value: Twice as far away, and the angle between its ends is about half as big.

data.name: Narr_Light_Angle_03
data.value: Your turn: move the car twenty metres away and see how small the angle gets.

data.name: Narr_Light_Angle_04
data.value: How big something looks is this angle. For a patch, like a lamp, it is how much of your view it fills.

data.name: Narr_Light_Sky_01
data.value: Stand on one spot of the floor and look up: a dome of sky, with the lamp right overhead.

data.name: Narr_Light_Sky_02
data.value: Press the dome flat into a circle. The lamp's patch is the share of light this spot gets.

data.name: Narr_Light_Sky_03
data.value: Bring the lamp down low. Its patch squashes thin near the rim, and the share drops.

data.name: Narr_Light_Sky_04
data.value: Your turn: move the lamp further away and watch its patch shrink.

data.name: Narr_Light_Sky_05
data.value: Which lamp gives this spot more light?

data.name: Light_Sky_Quiz1
data.value: A far lamp, low in the sky

data.name: Narr_Light_Radiance_01
data.value: A glowing panel, straight in front of the eye, two metres away.

data.name: Narr_Light_Radiance_02
data.value: Step back to four metres. Each bit sends you less, but you take in four times as much of the panel, so it looks just as bright.

data.name: Narr_Light_Radiance_03
data.value: Your turn: turn the panel away at a slant, and check whether it looks darker.

data.name: Narr_Light_Radiance_04
data.value: You walk twice as far away from a lit wall. How bright does it look?

data.name: Narr_Light_Reflection_01
data.value: A perfect mirror: the light leaves at the same angle it came in, all in one direction.

data.name: Narr_Light_Reflection_02
data.value: Move the eye away from that direction, and the mirror sends it nothing at all.

data.name: Narr_Light_Reflection_03
data.value: Now make the surface fully matte, like paper. The light scatters every way, so the eye sees the spot from anywhere.

data.name: Narr_Light_Reflection_04
data.value: Your turn: set the roughness in between, like glossy paint.

data.name: Narr_Light_Reflection_05
data.value: Which surface shows a bright highlight that moves when you move?

data.name: Narr_Light_Shadow_01
data.value: A tiny lamp over a box. Each spot of the floor sees all of it or none of it, so the shadow's edge is sharp.

data.name: Narr_Light_Shadow_02
data.value: Make the lamp big. Near the edge, part of the lamp is hidden and part is not, so the shadow fades gently.

data.name: Narr_Light_Shadow_03
data.value: Your turn: raise the lamp as high as it goes. Does the edge get sharper or softer?

data.name: Narr_Light_Shadow_04
data.value: Why are shadows so soft on a cloudy day?

data.name: Light_Shadow_Quiz2
data.value: The whole bright sky is one huge lamp

data.name: Narr_Light_Bounce_01
data.value: No bounces: only what the lamp reaches is lit, and the box's far side is pitch black.

data.name: Narr_Light_Bounce_02
data.value: One bounce. Lit surfaces light each other, and the floor by the red wall picks up a red glow.

data.name: Narr_Light_Bounce_03
data.value: Your turn: paint the wall blue and watch the glow on the floor change.

data.name: Narr_Light_Bounce_04
data.value: Three bounces. Each one adds less than the last, and the shadows fill in.

data.name: Narr_Light_Bounce_05
data.value: Why is the shade in a room never pitch black?

data.name: Light_Bounce_Quiz1
data.value: Light bounces off the walls into it

data.name: Narr_Gears_Ratio_01
data.value: Two gears with the same number of teeth: they turn at the same speed, in opposite directions.

data.name: Narr_Gears_Ratio_02
data.value: Give the right gear twice the teeth. Now it turns once for every two turns of the small one.

data.name: Narr_Gears_Ratio_03
data.value: Your turn: give the driven gear three times as many teeth as the driver.

data.name: Narr_Gears_Ratio_04
data.value: A ten-tooth gear drives a thirty-tooth gear. One turn of the small gear turns the big one how far?

data.name: Narr_Gears_Torque_01
data.value: The crank turns a small gear, and the small gear turns the drum's big gear.

data.name: Narr_Gears_Torque_02
data.value: Make the drum's gear bigger. The drum turns more slowly.

data.name: Narr_Gears_Torque_03
data.value: The drum now turns more slowly than the crank. What does it get in return?

data.name: Narr_Gears_Torque_04
data.value: Slower but stronger, or faster but weaker: gears trade one for the other, but never make energy from nothing.

data.name: Gears_Torque_Quiz1
data.value: It turns harder, so it lifts more

data.name: Narr_Gears_Involute_01
data.value: A string wound round a can, with a pencil tied to its end.

data.name: Narr_Gears_Involute_02
data.value: Your turn: unwind the string at least halfway round and watch the curve the pencil draws.

data.name: Narr_Gears_Involute_03
data.value: The tight string always meets the curve at a right angle. That is the curve on both sides of a good gear tooth.

data.name: Narr_Gears_Involute_04
data.value: With this shape, two teeth always push along one straight line, so the gears turn smoothly.

data.name: Narr_Gears_Mesh_01
data.value: The gears turn slowly. Watch the gold dot where two teeth touch.

data.name: Narr_Gears_Mesh_02
data.value: The dot slides along one slanted line, from where the teeth meet to where they let go.

data.name: Narr_Gears_Mesh_03
data.value: Speed it up. Before one pair lets go, the next pair has already met, so the push never stops.

data.name: Narr_Gears_Mesh_04
data.value: Your turn: make the pressure angle bigger and look at the teeth.

data.name: Narr_Gears_Mesh_05
data.value: What does a bigger pressure angle give the teeth?

data.name: Narr_Gears_Train_01
data.value: One step: a small gear drives a big one, and the speed drops three times.

data.name: Narr_Gears_Train_02
data.value: Two steps: a small gear fixed to the big one drives the next big gear. Three times three is nine.

data.name: Narr_Gears_Train_03
data.value: With three steps, how many times slower is the last gear?

data.name: Narr_Gears_Train_04
data.value: Your turn: add a fourth step and see how slowly the last gear creeps.

data.name: Narr_Gears_Planet_01
data.value: The ring is held still. Turn the sun, and the planets roll round it, taking the carrier slowly with them.

data.name: Narr_Gears_Planet_02
data.value: That is a big slowing in a small space, with no gear sticking out to the side.

data.name: Narr_Gears_Planet_03
data.value: Your turn: hold the carrier instead, and watch which way the ring turns.

data.name: Narr_Gears_Planet_04
data.value: Now the sun is held. The same gears give yet another speed.

data.name: Narr_Gears_Planet_05
data.value: How does a gearbox like this change its speed?

data.name: Gears_Planet_Quiz1
data.value: By holding a different part still

data.name: Narr_Watch_Spring_01
data.value: The mainspring has almost run down. It lies loose against the barrel wall.

data.name: Narr_Watch_Spring_02
data.value: Your turn: wind the spring all the way up, as the crown would.

data.name: Narr_Watch_Spring_03
data.value: Wound tight round the arbor, the spring pushes the barrel round, and the barrel's teeth drive the watch for about forty hours.

data.name: Narr_Watch_Spring_04
data.value: Where does a mechanical watch get its energy?

data.name: Narr_Watch_Hands_01
data.value: At real speed, the seconds hand sweeps round, and the other hands seem to stand still.

data.name: Narr_Watch_Hands_02
data.value: Sixty times faster: the minute hand now goes round once a minute.

data.name: Narr_Watch_Hands_03
data.value: Your turn: speed time up as far as it goes and watch the hour hand move.

data.name: Narr_Watch_Hands_04
data.value: Which hand is not carried by the going train itself?

data.name: Narr_Watch_Escape_01
data.value: In slow motion: the lever holds the escape wheel still with one red stone.

data.name: Narr_Watch_Escape_02
data.value: The balance swings past the middle and flicks the lever across. One stone lets go, the wheel jumps, the other stone catches it. Tick.

data.name: Narr_Watch_Escape_03
data.value: As the tooth slips past the stone, it gives the lever a small push, and the lever passes it on to the balance.

data.name: Narr_Watch_Escape_04
data.value: Your turn: speed the slow motion up and watch the ticks come faster.

data.name: Narr_Watch_Escape_05
data.value: What keeps the balance swinging, hour after hour?

data.name: Watch_Escape_Quiz1
data.value: A small push from the escape wheel each beat

data.name: Narr_Watch_Balance_01
data.value: The balance swings wide, to and fro, about two and a half times a second.

data.name: Narr_Watch_Balance_02
data.value: Now the swing is much narrower, as when the spring is nearly run down.

data.name: Narr_Watch_Balance_03
data.value: The swing got narrower. Does the watch slow down?

data.name: Narr_Watch_Balance_04
data.value: Your turn: make the hairspring a little stiffer and read how much the watch gains a day.

data.name: Narr_Watch_Balance_05
data.value: A tiny change in the spring is minutes a day, which is why watchmakers adjust it so carefully.

data.name: Watch_Balance_Quiz2
data.value: No: each swing still takes the same time

data.name: Narr_Watch_Rotor_01
data.value: The wrist moves, and the heavy rotor swings so that it keeps hanging down.

data.name: Narr_Watch_Rotor_02
data.value: With the reverser, both directions of swing wind the mainspring.

data.name: Narr_Watch_Rotor_03
data.value: Your turn: take the reverser out and watch the winding.

data.name: Narr_Watch_Rotor_05
data.value: Put it back. And once the spring is full, the barrel lets it slip instead of breaking it.

data.name: Watch_Rotor_Quiz3
data.value: Only one way of swinging winds the spring

data.name: Narr_Watch_Movement_01
data.value: The whole movement, put together. From here you only see the dial and hands.

data.name: Narr_Watch_Movement_02
data.value: Pull it apart into layers: the main plate, the barrel, the going train, the escapement and balance, the motion works and the dial.

data.name: Narr_Watch_Movement_03
data.value: The dial is hidden now, so you can see the wheels under it.

data.name: Narr_Watch_Movement_04
data.value: Your turn: hide the motion works too.

data.name: Narr_Watch_Movement_05
data.value: Energy flows from the spring at the bottom, up through each layer, to the hands at the top.

data.name: Narr_Light_Brightness_Part_Lamp
data.value: The lamp turns electricity into light. Its power, in watts, says how much light it sends out each second.

data.name: Narr_Light_Brightness_Part_Floor
data.value: The floor sends back some of the light that lands on it. That is the light that reaches your eye.

data.name: Narr_Light_Brightness_Part_Chart
data.value: Across is how much light there is, up is how bright it looks. The curve climbs fast, then flattens, then stops at white.

data.name: Narr_Light_Tilt_Part_Torch
data.value: The torch sends down a beam of the same width and the same amount of light, whatever the board does.

data.name: Narr_Light_Tilt_Part_Patch
data.value: The part of the board the beam lands on. The longer it gets, the less light each bit of it has.

data.name: Narr_Light_Tilt_Part_Board
data.value: Tip the board and the same beam is spread along more of it, like sunlight in the evening.

data.name: Narr_Light_Distance_Part_Lamp
data.value: A lamp so small it is nearly a point. Its light goes out in straight lines in every direction.

data.name: Narr_Light_Distance_Part_Square
data.value: Follow only the light that passes through this square. It never gains or loses any on the way.

data.name: Narr_Light_Distance_Part_Frame
data.value: The light from the gold square, now spread over more squares. Twice as far, four times the squares.

data.name: Narr_Light_Angle_Part_Car
data.value: The car is always four and a half metres long. Only its distance from the eye changes.

data.name: Narr_Light_Angle_Part_Arc
data.value: The angle between the lines to the car's two ends. This, not the car's length, is how big it looks.

data.name: Narr_Light_Angle_Part_View
data.value: The car as the eye sees it: as wide as the angle it takes up.

data.name: Narr_Light_Sky_Part_Spot
data.value: Everything here is seen from this one spot, looking up.

data.name: Narr_Light_Sky_Part_Lamp
data.value: A square lamp hanging above the spot. Move it lower or further, and its patch of sky changes.

data.name: Narr_Light_Sky_Part_Patch
data.value: The lamp's patch of the dome, pressed straight down onto the floor. Its share of the circle is this spot's share of the light.

data.name: Narr_Light_Sky_Part_Circle
data.value: The whole half-sphere of sky, pressed flat into a circle on the floor.

data.name: Narr_Light_Radiance_Part_Eye
data.value: The eye takes in light from a narrow cone in front of it, whatever is there.

data.name: Narr_Light_Radiance_Part_Panel
data.value: A panel that glows evenly, like a lit wall or a screen.

data.name: Narr_Light_Radiance_Part_Seen
data.value: The part of the panel inside the eye's cone. Further away or slanted, it is bigger, but each bit sends less, just as much less.

data.name: Narr_Light_Reflection_Part_Lamp
data.value: Light arrives from this side and lands on the surface in the middle.

data.name: Narr_Light_Reflection_Part_Mirror
data.value: Where a perfect mirror would send all the light: out at the same angle it came in.

data.name: Narr_Light_Reflection_Part_Lobe
data.value: The further this shape reaches in a direction, the more light leaves that way.

data.name: Narr_Light_Reflection_Part_Eye
data.value: How bright the spot looks depends on how much light leaves towards the eye.

data.name: Narr_Light_Shadow_Part_Lamp
data.value: A glowing square. Make it bigger, or bring it lower, and the shadow's edge gets softer.

data.name: Narr_Light_Shadow_Part_Box
data.value: The box hides part of the lamp from the floor behind it.

data.name: Narr_Light_Shadow_Part_Edge
data.value: Here the floor sees part of the lamp, not all of it, so it is part dark.

data.name: Narr_Light_Bounce_Part_Lamp
data.value: The only thing that makes light here. Everything else only sends light on.

data.name: Narr_Light_Bounce_Part_Wall
data.value: The wall gives back mostly its own colour and keeps the rest.

data.name: Narr_Light_Bounce_Part_Floor
data.value: Once light bounces, the wall lights this floor too, and tints it with its colour.

data.name: Narr_Light_Bounce_Part_Box
data.value: Its far side gets no light from the lamp at all. Only bounced light reaches it.

data.name: Narr_Gears_Ratio_Part_Driver
data.value: The gear that is turned. Each of its teeth pushes one tooth of the other gear past.

data.name: Narr_Gears_Ratio_Part_Driven
data.value: The gear being pushed round. More teeth means more pushes for one turn, so it turns slower.

data.name: Narr_Gears_Torque_Part_Crank
data.value: Your hand turns this. It goes round fast but pushes gently.

data.name: Narr_Gears_Torque_Part_Drum
data.value: The big gear and the drum on its axle. It turns slowly but hard enough to wind up the rope.

data.name: Narr_Gears_Torque_Part_Load
data.value: The weight on the rope. It climbs as the drum winds.

data.name: Narr_Gears_Torque_Part_Bars
data.value: The crank turns faster, the drum turns harder, by the same number of times.

data.name: Narr_Gears_Involute_Part_Can
data.value: The circle the string is wound on. On a gear it is called the base circle.

data.name: Narr_Gears_Involute_Part_String
data.value: It always leaves the can along a straight line that just touches it, and always meets the curve square on.

data.name: Narr_Gears_Involute_Part_Pencil
data.value: The end of the string. As it unwinds, it draws the curve.

data.name: Narr_Gears_Involute_Part_Curve
data.value: The curve on each side of a good gear tooth.

data.name: Narr_Gears_Mesh_Part_Contact
data.value: Each gold dot is a pair of teeth pressing on each other right now.

data.name: Narr_Gears_Mesh_Part_Line
data.value: Every touching point slides along this one line. Its slant is the pressure angle.

data.name: Narr_Gears_Train_Part_Input
data.value: The first, fast gear. The train starts here.

data.name: Narr_Gears_Train_Part_Output
data.value: The last gear, with a pointer. Each step in between slows it three times more.

data.name: Narr_Gears_Planet_Part_Sun
data.value: The gear in the middle. The planets roll round it.

data.name: Narr_Gears_Planet_Part_Ring
data.value: A big ring with its teeth on the inside, holding all the planets.

data.name: Narr_Gears_Planet_Part_Carrier
data.value: The frame that holds the planets' axles. When the planets travel round, it turns with them.

data.name: Narr_Watch_Spring_Part_Barrel
data.value: A drum with teeth on its rim. The spring inside pushes it round, and its teeth drive the watch.

data.name: Narr_Watch_Spring_Part_Arbor
data.value: The axle in the middle. Winding turns it, and the spring's inner end is hooked to it.

data.name: Narr_Watch_Spring_Part_Gauges
data.value: How hard the spring pulls, and how many hours it can still run the watch.

data.name: Narr_Watch_Hands_Part_Dial
data.value: The seconds hand is on the fourth wheel, the minute hand on the centre wheel. The hour hand is geared down from the minute hand.

data.name: Narr_Watch_Hands_Part_Train
data.value: Each big wheel drives a small pinion on the next axle, so each axle turns faster than the one before.

data.name: Narr_Watch_Escape_Part_Wheel
data.value: The last wheel of the train. It is only let go half a tooth at a time.

data.name: Narr_Watch_Escape_Part_Lever
data.value: It rocks from side to side each time the balance swings past the middle.

data.name: Narr_Watch_Escape_Part_Stones
data.value: Two red jewels on the lever. One always holds the escape wheel still.

data.name: Narr_Watch_Escape_Part_Balance
data.value: It swings to and fro and sets the pace. Its pin flicks the lever as it passes.

data.name: Narr_Watch_Balance_Part_Balance
data.value: A small, heavy-rimmed wheel. The heavier its rim, the slower it swings.

data.name: Narr_Watch_Balance_Part_Hairspring
data.value: A hair-thin spiral spring that always pulls the balance back to the middle. Stiffer means faster.

data.name: Narr_Watch_Balance_Part_Trace
data.value: How far the balance is turned, moment by moment. Wide or narrow, each swing takes the same time.

data.name: Narr_Watch_Rotor_Part_Rotor
data.value: A heavy half-moon that swings freely on the centre. Gravity keeps it hanging down.

data.name: Narr_Watch_Rotor_Part_Wheel
data.value: It only ever turns one way, and each turn winds the spring a little.

data.name: Narr_Watch_Rotor_Part_Barrel
data.value: Where the mainspring is wound up and stored.

data.name: Narr_Watch_Rotor_Part_Reserve
data.value: How full the mainspring is. Once it is full, the spring slips instead of winding further.

data.name: Narr_Watch_Movement_Part_Plate
data.value: The base everything is built on. Its little red rubies are bearings for the axles.

data.name: Narr_Watch_Movement_Part_Barrel
data.value: The mainspring in its drum: where the energy starts.

data.name: Narr_Watch_Movement_Part_Train
data.value: The wheels that carry the spring's push up to the escapement, faster at each step.

data.name: Narr_Watch_Movement_Part_Escapement
data.value: They let the energy out in even beats, five a second.

data.name: Narr_Watch_Movement_Part_Motionworks
data.value: Small wheels under the dial that slow the minute hand twelve times for the hour hand.

data.name: Narr_Watch_Movement_Part_Dial
data.value: The only part you see from the front, at the end of the whole chain.

data.name: Picture_KeyHint
data.value: Arrow keys: pick a part · Enter: what it is · Esc: close
